All of those games appear on both PC and console. This means that they are inherently going to be limited to what the lesser system can do. I don't mean that the graphics will be the same; I mean that the design of the game itself has to be limited to something that they all can handle.

So for example, keyboard/mouse input isn't (normally) done on console. So if you're going to make something crossplatform, you have to consider that some people will only have a controller and because the two are irreconcilably different, it will limit how the user will be able to interact with your game.

With graphics, you have a similar situation. If you develop with a game engine that is cross-platform, you've severely hampered your game's graphics. The PC version may get higher resolution textures, but fundamentally, the rendering system is going to be something that makes a compromise so that it can still run on the lesser computing power of a console.

That isn't how a game engine or rendering elements of an engine works. You don't compromise unless you specifically target the lowest common denominator and then don't make any accommodations for better systems, building things that can scale up and down to suit the platform is the number one reason I mentioned the games above, they will run on really awful hardware and run very well while looking an awful lot better on better hardware. Scalability is the name of the game, being able to scale up to take advantage of better hardware is what sets PC gaming apart from consoles (right now).

If what you said was true every game would come out with the exact same visuals on every platform just so it could run on the worst like GTA4 did on the PS3, Rockstar turned off most if not all of the more screen tint, shadows, reflections, and motion blur so half its visual fidelity was lost in order to accommodate the weak hardware and less than ideal design (Red Dead Redemption has a similar issue). Dark Souls 1 is a good example of a game made with no accommodations for better platforms, its target was PS3 and while it does looks fine on PS3 it doesn't really do anything to take advantage of the 360's slightly better hardware and when it came to PC the only difference was it instead of an internal renderer of less than 1280x720 it actually had 1280x720 only (its actually a bitch to get it running well on poor PC hardware).

Internal renderer is a trick developers use to eek a bit more performance out of a system by rendering the game at lets say 1024×576 or less then doing a fast bilnear or bicubic stretch before outputting to a display at 720 or 1080. This also helps mask some aliasing without using heavy amounts of anti-aliasing filters, they'd still use some to tidy up the image a bit and its one of the big differences between the xbox360 and the PS3. Its basically penalty free on the 360 where as the PS3 needed an entirely new anti-aliasing filter to get anything close to parity with what can be done on a 360. Its generally not done on PC versions of games because its expected that the user can decide for him/herself what is an acceptable way to play the game.

You might compromise on game design in order to accommodate a console, limit the map sizes and its complexity in some way like how Max Payne3 had a lot of the game either take place in extremely detailed tiny gameplay areas separated by unskippable cutscenes or relatively large low detailed gameplay areas with slightly fewer cutscenes.
